solution:
Let O be the centre and let seg OM \(\perp\) chord AB, with M on AB. Then \(OM = 8\) cm.
The perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord, so \(AM = \frac{1}{2} \times AB = \frac{1}{2} \times 12 = 6\) cm.
In the right-angled \(\Delta OMA\), by Pythagoras' theorem,
\(OA^2 = OM^2 + AM^2 = 8^2 + 6^2 = 64 + 36 = 100\)
So \(OA = 10\) cm, which is the radius.
Diameter \(= 2 \times OA = 2 \times 10 = 20\) cm.

Let O be the centre, AB the chord and seg OM \(\perp\) chord AB, with M on AB.
Radius \(= OA = \frac{1}{2} \times 26 = 13\) cm.
The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so \(AM = \frac{1}{2} \times 24 = 12\) cm.
In the right-angled \(\Delta OMA\), by Pythagoras' theorem,
\(OM^2 = OA^2 - AM^2 = 13^2 - 12^2 = 169 - 144 = 25\)
So \(OM = 5\).
The distance of the chord from the centre is 5 cm.

Let O be the centre, AB the chord and seg OM \(\perp\) chord AB, with M on AB. Then \(OA = 34\) cm and \(OM = 30\) cm.
In the right-angled \(\Delta OMA\), by Pythagoras' theorem,
\(AM^2 = OA^2 - OM^2 = 34^2 - 30^2 = 1156 - 900 = 256\)
So \(AM = 16\) cm.
The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so \(AB = 2 \times AM = 2 \times 16 = 32\).
The length of the chord is 32 cm.

Let seg OM \(\perp\) chord PQ, with M on PQ. Then \(OP = 41\) units.
The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so \(PM = \frac{1}{2} \times PQ = \frac{1}{2} \times 80 = 40\) units.
In the right-angled \(\Delta OMP\), by Pythagoras' theorem,
\(OM^2 = OP^2 - PM^2 = 41^2 - 40^2 = 1681 - 1600 = 81\)
So \(OM = 9\).
The distance of the chord from the centre is 9 units.

Draw seg OM \(\perp\) line AB, with M on AB. The same segment OM is perpendicular to seg PQ as well, because P and Q lie on line AB.
For the bigger circle, AB is a chord and OM \(\perp\) AB. The perpendicular drawn from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.
So \(AM = BM\) ..... (i)
For the smaller circle, PQ is a chord and OM \(\perp\) PQ. By the same property,
\(PM = QM\) ..... (ii)
The points lie on the chord in the order A, P, Q, B, so
\(AP = AM - PM\) and \(BQ = BM - QM\).
Subtracting (ii) from (i), \(AM - PM = BM - QM\).
Therefore \(AP = BQ\).

Let PQ be a diameter of the circle with centre O, and let it bisect the chords AB and CD at the points M and N respectively. (Neither chord is itself a diameter, otherwise its midpoint would be the centre O.)
Given: \(AM = BM\), so M is the midpoint of chord AB; and \(CN = DN\), so N is the midpoint of chord CD.
The segment joining the centre of a circle to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to that chord.
So seg OM \(\perp\) chord AB and seg ON \(\perp\) chord CD.
Now O, M and N all lie on the diameter PQ, so seg OM and seg ON both lie along line PQ.
Therefore line PQ \(\perp\) AB and line PQ \(\perp\) CD.
Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel to each other.
Hence chord AB \(\parallel\) chord CD, that is, the two chords are parallel.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(12\) cm, which is impossible for this question and is self-refuting on the stem's own numbers. The radius is \(10\) cm, so a line \(12\) cm from the centre misses the circle altogether — \(r^{2} - d^{2} = 100 - 144 < 0\) — and there is no chord at that distance to speak of. The perpendicular from the centre bisects a \(16\) cm chord into halves of \(8\), so \(d^{2} = 10^{2} - 8^{2} = 36\) and the distance is \(6\) cm; that value returns the stem's own chord, \(2\sqrt{100 - 36} = 16\) cm. The key's \(12\) is \(6 + 6\), the distance BETWEEN the two chords when they lie on opposite sides of the centre — the answer to a question this stem does not ask, since it asks for the distance of each chord FROM THE CENTRE.]

Let O be the centre, AB one of the chords and seg OM \(\perp\) chord AB, with M on AB.
The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so \(AM = \frac{1}{2} \times 16 = 8\) cm, and \(OA = 10\) cm.
In the right-angled \(\Delta OMA\), by Pythagoras' theorem,
\(OM^2 = OA^2 - AM^2 = 10^2 - 8^2 = 100 - 64 = 36\)
So \(OM = 6\) cm.
The two chords are congruent, and congruent chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre.
Each of the two chords is at a distance of 6 cm from the centre.

Let O be the centre, AB one of the chords and seg OM \(\perp\) chord AB, with M on AB. Then \(OA = 13\) cm and \(OM = 5\) cm.
In the right-angled \(\Delta OMA\), by Pythagoras' theorem,
\(AM^2 = OA^2 - OM^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144\)
So \(AM = 12\) cm.
The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so \(AB = 2 \times 12 = 24\) cm.
The chords are equal and are at the same distance from the centre, so the other chord has the same length.
The length of each chord is 24 cm.

Draw seg CM, seg CN and seg CP.
In \(\Delta PMC\) and \(\Delta PNC\),
seg PM \(\cong\) seg PN ..... (given)
seg CM \(\cong\) seg CN ..... (radii of the same circle)
seg PC \(\cong\) seg PC ..... (common side)
So \(\Delta PMC \cong \Delta PNC\) by the SSS test.
Corresponding angles of congruent triangles are congruent, so \(\angle MPC \cong \angle NPC\).
Ray PC lies in the interior of \(\angle NPM\) and divides it into two congruent angles.
Therefore ray PC is the bisector of \(\angle NPM\).
diagramNote: Circle with centre C; chords PM and PN drawn from a common point P on the circle, with radii CM, CN and the segment PC drawn, showing the two triangles PMC and PNC.

solution:
Here BC is the side included between \(\angle\)B and \(\angle\)C, so the triangle is constructed by the ASA (two angles and the included side) case.
Steps of construction:
(1) Draw seg BC of length 6.4 cm.
(2) At B, draw ray BX making \(\angle\)XBC \(= 100^\circ\).
(3) At C, on the same side of BC, draw ray CY making \(\angle\)YCB \(= 50^\circ\).
(4) Ray BX and ray CY intersect at A. \(\Delta\)ABC is the required triangle. (Its third angle is \(\angle\)A \(= 180^\circ - 100^\circ - 50^\circ = 30^\circ\).)
(5) Draw the bisector of \(\angle\)B and the bisector of \(\angle\)C. Let them intersect at I. Point I is the incentre.
(6) From I draw seg IP \(\perp\) seg BC, with P on BC.
(7) With centre I and radius IP, draw a circle. This circle touches all three sides of the triangle from inside and is the required incircle.
diagramNote: Triangle ABC with BC = 6.4 cm at the base, angle B = 100 degrees, angle C = 50 degrees; the bisectors of angles B and C meeting at I, the perpendicular IP to BC, and the incircle centred at I touching all three sides.

solution:
QR is the side included between \(\angle\)Q and \(\angle\)R, but \(\angle\)Q is not given, so first find it from the angle sum:
\(\angle\)Q \(= 180^\circ - \angle P - \angle R = 180^\circ - 70^\circ - 50^\circ = 60^\circ\).
Now the triangle can be drawn by the ASA case using \(\angle\)Q, QR and \(\angle\)R.
Steps of construction:
(1) Draw seg QR of length 7.3 cm.
(2) At Q, draw ray QX making \(\angle\)XQR \(= 60^\circ\).
(3) At R, on the same side of QR, draw ray RY making \(\angle\)YRQ \(= 50^\circ\).
(4) Ray QX and ray RY intersect at P. \(\Delta\)PQR is the required triangle.
(5) Draw the perpendicular bisector of seg PQ and the perpendicular bisector of seg QR. Let them intersect at O. Point O is the circumcentre, and it is equidistant from P, Q and R.
(6) With centre O and radius OQ, draw a circle. It passes through all three vertices P, Q and R and is the required circumcircle.
diagramNote: Triangle PQR with QR = 7.3 cm at the base, angle Q = 60 degrees, angle R = 50 degrees; perpendicular bisectors of PQ and QR meeting at the circumcentre O, and the circumcircle through P, Q, R.

solution:
All three sides are given, so the triangle is constructed by the SSS case. (The construction is possible because the sum of any two sides exceeds the third: \(5.8 + 6.7 = 12.5 > 6.9\).)
Steps of construction:
(1) Draw seg XY of length 6.7 cm.
(2) With centre Y and radius 5.8 cm, draw an arc.
(3) With centre X and radius 6.9 cm, draw another arc cutting the first arc at Z.
(4) Draw seg XZ and seg YZ. \(\Delta\)XYZ is the required triangle.
(5) Draw the bisector of \(\angle\)X and the bisector of \(\angle\)Y. Let them intersect at I. Point I is the incentre.
(6) From I draw seg IP \(\perp\) seg XY, with P on XY.
(7) With centre I and radius IP, draw a circle. This circle touches all three sides of the triangle from inside and is the required incircle.
diagramNote: Triangle XYZ with XY = 6.7 cm, YZ = 5.8 cm, XZ = 6.9 cm drawn by arcs; the bisectors of angles X and Y meeting at I, the perpendicular IP to XY, and the incircle centred at I touching all three sides.

solution:
\(\angle\)M is the angle included between side LM and side MN, so the triangle is constructed by the SAS (two sides and the included angle) case.
Steps of construction:
(1) Draw seg MN of length 6.4 cm.
(2) At M, draw ray MX making \(\angle\)XMN \(= 105^\circ\).
(3) On ray MX, mark point L such that \(ML = 7.2\) cm.
(4) Draw seg LN. \(\Delta\)LMN is the required triangle.
(5) Draw the perpendicular bisector of seg LM and the perpendicular bisector of seg MN. Let them intersect at O. Point O is the circumcentre.
(6) With centre O and radius OM, draw a circle. It passes through L, M and N and is the required circumcircle.
Note: \(\angle\)M \(= 105^\circ\) is obtuse, so the triangle is obtuse-angled and the circumcentre O lies outside the triangle, on the side of seg LN opposite to M.
diagramNote: Obtuse triangle LMN with MN = 6.4 cm, angle M = 105 degrees, LM = 7.2 cm; perpendicular bisectors of LM and MN meeting at the circumcentre O lying OUTSIDE the triangle beyond seg LN, and the circumcircle through L, M, N.

solution:
In \(\Delta\)DEF, \(DE = EF\), so the angles opposite these sides are equal, that is \(\angle D = \angle F = 45^\circ\).
Then \(\angle E = 180^\circ - 45^\circ - 45^\circ = 90^\circ\), and EF is the side included between \(\angle\)E and \(\angle\)F, so the triangle can be drawn by the ASA case.
Steps of construction:
(1) Draw seg EF of length 6 cm.
(2) At F, draw ray FX making \(\angle\)XFE \(= 45^\circ\).
(3) At E, on the same side of EF, draw ray EY making \(\angle\)YEF \(= 90^\circ\).
(4) Ray FX and ray EY intersect at D. \(\Delta\)DEF is the required triangle. On measuring, \(DE = 6\) cm, as required.
(5) Draw the perpendicular bisector of seg DE and the perpendicular bisector of seg EF. Let them intersect at O. Point O is the circumcentre.
(6) With centre O and radius OE, draw a circle. It passes through D, E and F and is the required circumcircle.
Note: since \(\angle E = 90^\circ\), seg DF is a diameter of this circle and O is the midpoint of seg DF.
diagramNote: Right isosceles triangle DEF with EF = 6 cm, angle F = 45 degrees, angle E = 90 degrees, DE = 6 cm; perpendicular bisectors of DE and EF meeting at O, which is the midpoint of the hypotenuse DF, and the circumcircle through D, E, F.
